$comment: The kit's own canaries. A template that ships broken replicates across every project that copies it, so these run in CI on this repo.

canaries.guards: The tempting repair when the shared rules document tripped the share-mount guard was to stop scanning markdown. Prose is in scope on purpose: a README telling someone to mount a share is a deploy path even though it cannot execute. Only the fleet's own rules document, identical in every repository and incapable of carrying a project's deploy instructions, is excused.
The backlog validator rejects a symptom too short to act on. Without this an entry can say 'broken' and still count as a tracked bug.

A dated deferral is listed once it passes. Without this, 'revisit before the next release' becomes permanent by accident: the date no longer fails a pull request, so being told about it is all that is left.

A lapsed reviewBy prints a warning and leaves check-backlog's exit code alone. It used to fail every pull request on the day the date passed, and on 2026-10-16 failed gorfednet/.github#55 for seven entries it did not touch (the 2026-10 right-sizing: a pull request check fails only on something that pull request can change).
A gap or duplicate in a rule sequence fails the build. Nine branches merging at once once produced 21-24 missing and two rules both numbered 25, with registry entries citing rules that had moved.
A source glob matching nothing fails rather than certifying that every citation resolves. Every assertion in that check is vacuously true of an empty file list.
A staleness check that cannot reach the canonical manifest fails. Passing there would report 'current' during an outage — the silent-green shape the whole kit exists to find.
A kit file edited in a consuming project fails. Otherwise it is a fix fifteen projects will not get, and a divergence the next refresh silently overwrites.
A reusable pr-check workflow that does not run the verification gate fails. Otherwise the project that adopts it gets a green check over nothing checked.
A step in the verification gate without `if: !cancelled()` fails. GitHub defaults a step to success(), so an unrelated earlier failure switches the assertion off at exactly the moment it matters.
canaries.find:
- name: No generated files tracked in git
      if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
canaries.replace: - name: No generated files tracked in git

canaries.guards: A registry entry that has not been re-verified inside the window is reported by the audit. The offline run no longer fails on it (a pull request cannot change the date), so the warning is the whole remaining signal: without it, a table of intentions keeps reading as authoritative.

A repository lookup that failed for a reason other than 404 is reported, not treated as evidence either way. Collapsing it to 'absent' cries wolf during an outage; collapsing it to 'present' certifies a tier nobody checked.
The readable fleet table cannot disagree with the checked one. A generated file nobody regenerates is a hand-maintained list wearing a disguise.
A non-GitHub remote returns null rather than a plausible-looking slug that would send API calls somewhere they cannot succeed.

A repository the credentials cannot open must not fall through to the absent branch. GitHub answers 404 both for a private repository the caller may not see and for a path that is genuinely missing, and conflating the two made the first online run of this check accuse a fully-adopted project of holding none of the kit. Rule V39.

Nine production sites are watched by one reusable workflow, whose Playwright step used to exit 0 when the spec file was absent. Renaming a spec silently ended live monitoring and printed a tick. Asking for the smoke and not having it must fail; not wanting it is run-playwright: false, which a reader can see in the caller.
canaries.find:
echo "::error::run-playwright is true but $spec does not exist." \
                 "Point smoke-spec at the real file, or set run-playwright: false" \
                 "and accept that nothing is watching this site's behaviour."
            exit 1

canaries.guards: A status code says a server answered, not that it served the site. The body size floor and the expected-text match are what separate a live site from a parking page, a CDN error page, or an empty 200 from a broken deploy.
Callers list sitemap.xml and robots.txt beside HTML. The byte floor is an HTML budget; applying it to a 512-byte sitemap is how gorfed.net went red on 2026-09-21 while the site was up.

An input a project can set that the gate never receives. The configuration reads as applied and does nothing, which is worse than not offering it. source-dirs was added to the assertion and not to the generator that writes these workflows, so the script the test recommends produced a workflow that failed the test.

V46. The naive main-module idiom compares a resolved file URL to a raw argv path. Through a symlinked directory they differ, the CLI never runs, and the process exits 0 — a checker reporting success having checked nothing. It was in two of this kit binaries, including the one CI uses to verify the manifest.

V48's checker giving a verdict without a denominator. Its first version printed a green tick having measured six jobs in a repository that declares forty, reporting 'all under 75% of their timeout' while examining none of the ones anyone worried about.

V50. The jobs endpoint pages at 30 and reports the truth only in total_count. Reading page one and calling it the run drops exactly the jobs this check exists to watch, since matrix legs are what push a run past thirty — and coverage still counts the declaration as seen from page one, so the verdict is green over a truncated sample.

The drift checker warns and exits 0 one release behind, rather than failing. Without this the commonest situation is a red build, the fleet reads the red as noise, and a locally modified kit hides inside it.
The tolerance for being behind expires on a date. Without this an undated leniency becomes permanent by accident and the fail-above-one-minor half never fires.

check-backlog --verify-prs fails when an entry and its pull request disagree. Without this the plan of record can claim in-review against a merged PR indefinitely, which six entries across the fleet did.
assert-tests-executed names each test that only passed on a retry. Without this the run prints a count, exits 0, and the failing test is findable only by reading the JSON report by hand.

A citation is a number on the same line as the word rule. Without this a sentence ending in 'rules' above a line starting with a digit is reported as a dangling citation, and the repair is to weaken the checker.
The manifest writer takes an explicit release version. Without it the bump counts runs, and two runs in one change put every consumer more than one minor behind, which now fails rather than warns.

The tier-2 wiring check pairs a report and a floor within one mapping. Without the scoping it takes the first of each from the joined workflows, so an earlier empty report hides a real pair and a report in one job certifies a floor in another.
canaries.find: const sameBlock = (line, indent) => line.trim() === '' || indentOf(line) >= indent

canaries.guards: A test.fail() case — one asserting something is broken — is not reported as an intermittent failure. Counting any failed attempt as a retry made this check invent flakiness, and a repository with a budget of 0 would go red over tests behaving exactly as written.
A test that timed out and passed on the retry is named. The commonest intermittent shape there is, and the first version of the detector looked only for the literal status failed.

A rulebook section number such as comprehensive rules 1-2-1-1-1 is not read as citing local rule 1-2. A citation may no more be followed by -<digit> than by .<digit>, both being section numbers rather than rules. Anchored on that lookahead pair rather than on the whole pattern, because an anchor spanning the entire regex is invalidated by every narrowing — twice so far.

An impossible answer — a consumer ahead of canonical — is confirmed against an uncached read before it fails the build. Two repositories went red three minutes after a release because the CDN had not caught up, and a check that reddens for a reason unrelated to what it guards teaches that the check is noise.

The entry describing the pull request under review is exempt when written as landed, and refused when written as in-review. Without this there is no honest status for that entry: in-review is false the moment it merges and landed is false while it is open, so the default branch goes red after every merge and the gate stops being one.

A local prefix may contain a letter without beginning with one. 4thcltr.com uses 4C, so requiring a leading letter skipped its citations entirely — reporting that every citation resolves, which is the worse of the two directions a coverage matcher can fail in.

A number beginning with zero is not a citation, because no sequence starts at zero. towit.io vendors two copies of AngularJS whose pluralization comment says "three explicit number rules 0, 1 and 2", and the check is not wired there — so it was a false failure waiting for whoever wired it first.

The monitor's curl format ends with a newline. Without it `read` reports failure at EOF though it has assigned every variable, and under set -e the step dies before printing the URL it was checking — which took live monitoring for all nine sites down between 2026-09-07 and 2026-09-11 while looking like an infrastructure hiccup (V61).

Playwright's install runs under the same condition as the smoke that needs it. Mismatched, an earlier failure skips the install while the smoke proceeds, and the run's error becomes a missing npm package rather than the fault that occurred.
canaries.find:
- name: Setup Node for Playwright
        if: ${{ !cancelled() && inputs.run-playwright }}
canaries.replace:
- name: Setup Node for Playwright
        if: inputs.run-playwright

canaries.guards: The shared deploy writes into the existing inode. Without --inplace rsync renames a temp file over the target, and over the CIFS mount that serves these sites the container keeps a handle to the deleted inode: every request for that path then returns 500 until the container is restarted. It does not expire, and a reload does not clear it (V61).

A caller passing --partial-dir is refused before rsync runs, because this helper always passes --inplace and rsync rejects that pair as a usage error. ssatcy.com's own transport had --partial-dir, and adding --inplace there stopped every deploy from that repository before a byte moved.

A failed rsync is the function's answer, whatever the steps after it would report. A caller writing `nas_ssh_rsync_to … || handle` disables errexit inside the function, so without an explicit status the live check's 200 became the verdict on a deploy that transferred nothing — found by pointing anal0g's prune at a source path that does not exist and watching it exit 0.
canaries.find:
if [[ "${status}" -ne 0 ]]; then
    echo "rsync exited ${status}. Not repairing permissions and not checking the" \
      "site, because neither would describe this deploy." >&2
    return "${status}"
  fi

canaries.guards: The post-deploy live check accepts a 200 or a redirect and nothing else. Widened to any answer at all, a 500 from the site reads as a successful deploy — which is how eleven sites came to be deployed with nothing asking whether they still served.
Deploying a fleet domain fetches the site by itself. A verification each repository has to opt into is one that some repository will not have, and this fleet has ten deploy scripts.
A site that does not serve fails the deploy. Returning success from the check leaves the operator's last line reading "Deploy complete", which is the precise shape of the outage this rule came from.

The live URL is read from fleet.json rather than guessed from the directory name, so a staging target like bindercurve.com-dev is not probed at a hostname nobody serves and then reported as a broken deploy.

The drift check compares the shared documents the kit distributes from outside its own directory. Without it nothing hashed docs/verification-rules.md at all: bindercurve.com's copy held two rules canonical did not have — numbered in the shared sequence, which the next fleet rule then collided with — and was missing paragraphs canonical did have, while its drift check printed a tick.

The drift check compares versions before accepting matching hashes as current. Without that ordering it exited on the hashes alone, so the behind, far-behind and grace-date logic never ran: a release that changed only the shared documents left every consumer hash-clean, version-behind, and reported as up to date indefinitely — a check that could not fail, inside the tool built to find that shape elsewhere.

refresh-kit writes the shared documents as well as the kit files. It is the remedy every drift message prints, so a refresh that only writes kit files leaves the failure it was named for in place — a remedy that cannot reach green is decoration.

write-manifest refuses to write a manifest that omits a named shared document. Omitting one silently is a document the whole fleet stops comparing, and the omission looks exactly like having nothing to compare.
canaries.replace:
if (!existsSync(path)) { continue } else if (false) {
      // Fail rather than omit.

canaries.guards: A bare `rule 12` cites the shared document whether or not the project also keeps local rules. When it addressed whichever list the project numbered its own rules in, adopting a local prefix silently rewrote every citation already in the repository: bindercurve.com added two local rules and 34 citations across six files stopped resolving in one commit.
canaries.find:
const cited = Number(raw)
    if (cited < 1 || cited > sharedNumbers.length) {

canaries.guards: A pull-request check drops an argument it does not recognise. `--repo=gorfednet/4thcltr.com` was dropped that way, the check fell back to the clone it ran in, and bindercurve.com #95's review findings were reported as 4thcltr.com #95's.
GITHUB_REPOSITORY is skipped and the clone's origin answers instead. Run from the bindercurve.com clone with GITHUB_REPOSITORY=gorfednet/4thcltr.com, the check reported on bindercurve.com #95.

The monthly fleet report lists backlog entries whose reviewBy has passed. Those dates used to fail every pull request on the day they lapsed; now they are only told about, so a report that stops listing them leaves nothing that notices a review date going by.

A 404 or 403 from a repository's Actions workflow list, after the repository itself was read, means the token cannot see Actions: that list answers 200 and empty when there are none. Read as absence, a token without Actions access made the first audit report a quiet, green fleet (Bugbot on #43, V39).

The report probes a repository's root listing before reading a missing workflow directory or backlog as absent. Without the probe, a token that cannot read files, or an outage, reports a repository as having no workflows and no backlog, and exits 0 (V39).
Each workflow is judged by its own last completed run on main. Judging the newest run reads one still in progress as the result, which hid a failed last completion behind it (Bugbot on #43).

A run whose jobs failed without running a step counts as started. While bindercurve.com's account payment was failing, every job on #327 and #333 to #339 concluded failure with zero steps and the check said all started, so a branch nobody tested read as a broken one.

The workflow list is paged until its total_count, and a list that ends short of it is a failure. Judging main from one page of results let a failed workflow that fell off the page leave main reading green (Bugbot on #43).

A failed listing of .github/workflows is a lookup the report could not make, so the run goes red. It used to be written as unavailable on the gate line and as 'no healthcheck workflow' on the next, with exit 0 (Bugbot on #43).
A workflow file that could not be read may be the one that calls the shared gate, so the gate line is undetermined and the run red. It used to be a note beside 'does not call gorfednet/.github'.

A push workflow with only tag filters runs on tags and on nothing else, so its stale runs on the default branch are not the branch's health. Treating it as an unfiltered push made milestone-release read 'not green' on bindercurve.com for a failure from before it became tag-only.

Only workflows that run on a push to the branch or on a schedule speak for main. Judging every active workflow by its last run on the branch let a manual-only workflow's one-off failure (ops-nginx-restore-prod, 2026-09-15) hold main red.

A workflow whose triggers could not be read is undetermined for main and the run goes red. Dropping it from both lists would be a workflow skipped silently, which is how a guard reads clean about what it could not look at.
canaries.find: unknown: `could not read what triggers it (${cause.message})`,

canaries.guards: A workflow GitHub still registers but whose file is only on another branch cannot run from a push to the default branch or its schedule. Reading its file by path, or judging it, turned subrythm.com's gate-ref-test into a red audit run (2026-10-10). The directory listing is the whole directory, so a path missing from it is not on the branch.

The healthcheck line uses the same trigger classification as the main verdict. A reusable-only production-healthcheck (gorfednet/.github) has no runs of its own on main; reporting 'has no completed run' read as a healthcheck that had never run.

A deploy hard-links unchanged files from the current release with a destination-relative --link-dest. Without it every release is a full copy and the retention window multiplies the disk use of each site.
Retention never deletes the release `current` points at, however old. Rolling current back to an old release and then deploying again would otherwise delete the live site.
A live check that finds the site serving other bytes switches current back to the previous release. Without it a bad deploy stays live and the script only complains.
An empty release is refused even where the index.html check is waived. An empty directory behind current serves 403 for the whole site.

A deploy refuses an upload whose .build-sha is not HEAD. On 2026-10-20 gorfmusic.com's deploy.sh was run without a build: the source was origin/main, dist/ was the morning's build, and /privacy went live as a 404.
A site fleet.json marks buildStamp cannot deploy an upload with no .build-sha. Without it a build that never wrote the stamp (or a deploy.sh run with no build) goes out unchecked.

check-links fails a #fragment the target page has no id for. A page that exists answers 200 for any fragment, so a renamed heading id breaks every contents list and cross-link pointing at it with nothing else noticing.
check-links follows url() in every stylesheet. A font or background URL is never clicked, so a dropped font file ships as a silent fallback face and a 404 in every visitor's console.
check-html fails on every validator error and on a file the validator could not read. Classifying them as anything else turns the W3C check into a printout.
sync-report-issues closes an issue the latest run no longer sees. Left open, a fixed link stays listed as broken, and a label full of stale issues is one nobody reads.

report-outbound-links files only a 404, a 410, a dead name, a refused connection or a bad certificate. Filing a 403 would open an issue every week for every bank and retailer that refuses bots, while a visitor's browser gets the page.

A listed URL must be its own canonical to the character. Ignoring the trailing slash lets denseware.com and ssatcy.com pass: they listed /x/ while the page said /x, nginx 301s /x to /x/, and the client sent the reader back.

check-rules-drift fails on a retired term in a rule, skill, agent or memory file. Excusing every line that names a retired term turns the guard into a list of files it read and nothing else (plan row 5.4).

A file git still calls binary (a .gitattributes -diff line in the change) that gave no readable lines is read whole, not skipped and not refused. Skipped, the change switches its own check off for that file. --text alone no longer carries this: dropping it leaves the whole-file read, which is the reason this canary mutates the read and not the flag (plan row 1.30a review, 1.30f).
The allowlist comes from the base revision. Read from the head, a change that adds a path exemption for itself passes with private detail in it.
An added line that begins with ++ shows up as +++ and is content. Taken for a file header it drops the next lines, and a planted value after it passes.
A plain private address added to a file must fail the guard.
canaries.find: if (on('private-ip')) add('private-ip', all(PRIVATE_IP, svg ? stripSvgData(text) : text))
canaries.replace: if (false) add('private-ip', all(PRIVATE_IP, svg ? stripSvgData(text) : text))

canaries.guards: The workflow runs the guard from the base commit. Run from the head, a pull request that edits the script (for example to exit 0 at once) switches its own check off.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='merge base with full history' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A value counts as already held only when the same rule finds the same whole value in the base file. As a substring test, a file holding a longer public name lets a shorter private one through.
The commit log is split on NUL (git log -z). Split on a control character a message can hold, a message with that byte hides text from the scan and can print it as a sha.
No file is skipped by name. A text file called notes.png that holds a private address must still fail; skipping image names lets a change hide a value behind a file name it picks.
canaries.find: for (const { path, line, text } of added) {
canaries.replace:
for (const { path, line, text } of added) {
    if (/\.(?:png|ico|woff2?)$/i.test(path)) continue

canaries.guards: A merge commit is read for the added or renamed paths it wrote itself. Skipped, a file a merge adds by hand whose name holds a value passes.
A merge commit is read for new files in forbidden directories. Skipped, a runbook added inside a merge passes.
A merge commit is read for the lines it wrote itself. Skipped, a value hand-added in a merge and removed by the next commit passes.
A file whose own name holds a value is shown as a hash of its path. Printed, the value reaches the public log.
The allowlist can exempt one commit message. Ignored, a message with a value is red for good, because force push is denied.
A rename in a diff is known before its lines are read. Set after, a commit that renames a file and adds a value the file already held goes red with no way to clear it.
canaries.find: for (const f of files) if (f.from) origin.set(f.path, origin.get(f.from) ?? f.from)

canaries.guards: A file the merge base already holds is restored, not new. Called new, deleting and restoring a file under a forbidden directory goes red for good.
A bare name is watched only while the merge base has never said it. Always watched, nearly every mention of a site name is red, with no way out but a rewrite.
Started through a symlink, or under --preserve-symlinks-main, the script must still run. Compared by raw path it takes itself for an import and exits 0 having read nothing.
A deleted or purely renamed binary file has nothing to read. Treated as unread, the change can never pass.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='deleted or renamed file git calls binary' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A package version tag (a name, an at sign, then a dotted version) is not an address. Read as one, the check goes red on a package.json.
Numbers in minified SVG path data are not addresses. Read, a logo goes red.
A bare name in a commit message is a disclosure like any other.
A directory or a file named for a private repository discloses it.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='directory and as a file name' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A root commit that a merge brings in is diffed against the empty tree. A wrong id makes the diff fail, and the guard exits 2 on a branch that has one.
A bare name is read in every file, not only in list files: an unsaid name in prose, a YAML value or a command line is a disclosure.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='bare names, in more shapes' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A repo line in the allowlist names a name that is public already. For a name the repository never said it would disclose it with a green check.
A letter before a dotted number is no excuse: a flag, a host name, an escape. Excused, an address written right after a letter passes.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='take a version for an address' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: Drawing data is dropped only in an svg file or on a path tag. Dropped everywhere, an address can hide in a d or points attribute of any file.
A path with a quote, backslash or tab is C-quoted in a diff header. Not decoded, the count check fails for good, and the error can print the path.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='quote, a backslash or a tab' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A name the base only says inside a longer name or a host is still unsaid. Taken as said, a new list of bare names passes.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='longer name or a host' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: The owner-quote value ends at the closing quote. Run to the end of the line, editing text after a quote the base already holds goes red for good.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='owner quote in a file whose marker' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A v before a four-part address is not a version. Every private IPv4 address has four parts, so excusing a v let v10 and three more parts through.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='take a version for an address' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: Code punctuation before the date means code: a destructured owner beside n: 2 and a string is not a quote. Any text before the digit takes it for one.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='near misses that must stay clean' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: The colon shape skips owner as a key: first on its line, or after a brace or a comma. Without that, an object literal with a two-word value reads as a quote.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='near misses that must stay clean' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: An owner quote dated with an ordinal (7th November), a weekday, on, or a slashed date is still a quote. Read only as a day then a space, all four pass.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='owner quote with (an ordinal|a weekday|on before|a slashed)' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: An owner quote first on its line (a note, an indented bullet) is a quote. Only a key whose value ends the line with a comma or brace is code.
A key first on its line whose quoted value ends the line with a comma or a brace is an object literal, not a quote.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='near misses that must stay clean' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A name the base already says is public as a name, not as a private repository. A line that pairs it with private (the 14 November inventory: name, date, private) discloses that, and passes if said names are never read.
Private only as a whole word: privately or a_private_key beside a said name says nothing about which repositories are private.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='only as part of a word' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: An unsaid name written as a file name in prose (name.md) is the name. Read only as a bare word, it passes.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='a file name in prose' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: One file extension, then nothing: name.md.example.com is a host, not the name. Without the end check after the extension it reads as one.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='inside a host or before a second extension' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: name.wiki and name.wiki.git are the repository's wiki. Without the wiki suffix both pass.
An underscore is a boundary: name_notes and OLD_name say the name. Taken as part of a longer word, both pass.
main holds public design notes under docs/plans, and plan row 1.30 moves the plan of record, not those. Refused, every later design note PR goes red.

A commit line in main's allowlist exempts that commit's own diff. Ignored, a false positive in a commit that is not the tip is red for good: fixing forward leaves it in history, and force push is denied.

The allowlist is read from the base revision. Read from the merge base, a commit line merged to main after the branch forked does nothing until the branch merges main, so a stuck pull request stays red.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='allowlist PR merged after the branch forked' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A commit exemption names the full 40-hex id. A short prefix can be matched by a commit made to share it, which would exempt a leak.
A finding in a commit that is not the tip gets the full id and the allowlist way out. Without it, the advice is to rewrite a branch that cannot be force pushed.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='stays red after a fix forward' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A quoted path is decoded by code point. By code unit a character outside the BMP breaks, the diff path never matches the count, and the guard exits 2 for good.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='quote, a backslash or a tab' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A name listed as a site counts as said. Without it a README link or commit message naming the public domain is refused as a new private-repository name.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='lets the domain through in a README link' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A site line the allowlist's own diff cleared holds nothing for later lines. Without it, a second push of a comment or repo line naming the domain reads as held.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='holds nothing for a later line' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: The pre-push guard counts a site-listed name as said, as the CI guard does. Without it a README link to the public site is refused at push.

A single new `site <domain>` line the range adds counts for that range, so a repository with no allowlist can add its first line and link the site together. Without it the first line is refused and there is no way in.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='lets a repository add its first site line' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: Only one new site line per range clears. Without the cap, a push could link or name more than one new site elsewhere in the range. The allowlist's own site lines still publish each name they list.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='lets a repository add its first site line' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A site line is not read for its own domain, which is the only route for two or more new sites. Without it the allowlist lines themselves are refused.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='lets a repository add its first site line' test/privacyGuard.test.mjs

canaries.guards: The context-cap hook refuses new work at 200,001 tokens. Without it a session runs past the cap unheld, which is the waste plan row 1.61 names.
A policy change with the date untouched fails (V78). Without it the check passes every stale date.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='fails a policy change with the date left alone' templates/verification-kit/test/privacyDate.test.mjs

canaries.guards: Only a commit that changed the policy text supplies the required day. Without it a footer-only commit on a later day makes that day valid.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='counts only commits that change the policy text' templates/verification-kit/test/privacyDate.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A date moving backwards fails. Without it an old branch can date a policy change before the base date.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='fails a date that moves back' templates/verification-kit/test/privacyDate.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A PR may not change what counts as policy text (region, exclude, datePattern) in the same change as the page. Without it a widened exclude hides the edit and the date stays stale.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='widens exclude to hide the edit' templates/verification-kit/test/privacyDate.test.mjs

canaries.guards: A base config that does not parse fails the check. Without it both locks switch off for a PR that corrupts the config.
canaries.find: bail(`the base config ${renamedFrom ?? configRel} does not parse
canaries.replace: void (`the base config ${renamedFrom ?? configRel} does not parse

canaries.guards: An entry re-pointed at a copy is refused while the old page still exists. Without it a stale copy stands in for the page and a policy edit keeps its old date.
canaries.find: baseEntry && oldFile !== page.file && showAt(head, oldFile, cwd) !== null) {
canaries.replace: baseEntry && oldFile !== page.file && oldFile !== dateFile && showAt(head, oldFile, cwd) !== null) {

canaries.guards: Whether the page changed is decided by comparing blobs, so a ./ or non-ASCII path in the config still sees an edit. Without it every policy edit to such a page passes.
A dateFile change is refused in a PR that also touches the page. Without it a policy edit takes its date from any file holding today's date.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='dateFile change in a PR that also edits' templates/verification-kit/test/privacyDate.test.mjs

canaries.guards: The required day is the latest author day across policy-changing commits, not the last in log order. Without it a reordered or amended history demands an older day than the text visitors read.
canaries.command: node --test --test-name-pattern='latest author day across policy commits' templates/verification-kit/test/privacyDate.test.mjs
canaries.find: if (day === null || d > day) day = d

canaries.guards: With PRIVACY_DATE_ENFORCE unset a real problem prints ::warning and exits 0. Without it the warning-only ship condition is lost and a site job fails.
